title: Design Review & Architecture Discussion
description: Vocabulario de architecture reviews, RFCs y design docs de nivel senior/staff: trade-offs, non-goals, prior art, invariants, migration strategies y cómo defender o cuestionar un diseño con precisión técnica.

vocab.example: The trade-off is latency versus consistency — you can't have both here.
Non-goal: we're not addressing multi-region failover in this design.
The prior art here is Google's Spanner paper — worth reading before we finalize.

vocab.translation: sección del RFC con opciones descartadas
vocab.example: The 'alternatives considered' section explains why we ruled out event sourcing.
Migration tooling is out of scope for this doc — separate RFC to follow.

The first-order effect is faster reads; the second-order effect is more complex operations.

vocab.translation: grado de relación interna del módulo
vocab.example: The service has strong cohesion — every method is about ranking search results.

vocab.translation: movimiento de un estado a otro
vocab.example: The migration will run in three phases over six weeks.
Cutover is scheduled for Saturday at 02:00 UTC — low traffic window.

vocab.translation: migración de golpe (todo a la vez)
vocab.example: A big-bang migration is too risky at this scale — let's do it incrementally.
An incremental rollout lets us catch issues before they affect everyone.
Let's dry-run the migration on staging with production data first.

vocab.translation: réplica de tráfico real sin efecto
vocab.example: We'll mirror shadow traffic to the new service for a week to compare responses.
Dark launch first — the code path runs but the result isn't shown to users.

vocab.translation: misma funcionalidad que el sistema anterior
vocab.example: The v2 service needs feature parity with v1 before we can flip traffic over.
The gap analysis identified three missing endpoints and one behavioral difference.
On paper the algorithm is O(log n); in practice, cache misses dominate.

vocab.translation: componente crítico del que depende todo
vocab.example: This assumption is load-bearing for the whole design — if it breaks, the doc collapses.
We should minimize the API surface area — every method is a future maintenance burden.
The feature flag is our escape hatch if we need to disable this after launch.
The design covers the happy path well; failure modes deserve more thought.

vocab.translation: manera en que algo puede fallar
vocab.example: What's the failure mode if the coordinator dies mid-transaction?
Under load, we degrade gracefully by serving stale reads instead of failing.
In steady state we handle 5k RPS comfortably; the concern is traffic bursts.

listening.text: Have we considered event sourcing as an alternative? I'd like to see it in the 'alternatives considered' section.
What's the blast radius if the coordinator service fails? I don't see that discussed in the failure modes section.
Non-goal for this design: we're not solving multi-tenancy in this iteration — that's a separate RFC.
The trade-off you're proposing is consistency for availability. I'd like to see that stated explicitly at the top.

Back-of-the-envelope: at 10k requests per second and 2KB per payload, that's 20MB per second of network traffic per node.
I'd like to sanity check the assumption that reads outnumber writes by a hundred to one — where does that number come from?

This is the load-bearing assumption of the whole design. If it doesn't hold, we need a very different approach.
Feature parity with v1 is table stakes before we can even think about deprecating the old service.

speaking.target: The trade-off we made here is consistency for latency. We accept eventual consistency in exchange for sub-50-millisecond reads at the edge.
Help me understand why we chose a message queue over a synchronous RPC here. I'd expect the added complexity to need stronger justification.
I'm not blocking on this, but I'd like to flag a concern about the migration story — the cutover window feels optimistic.
The invariant we're preserving is that no write is ever lost, even in the presence of network partitions. Everything else in the design serves that goal.
We considered three alternatives — CRDT-based replication, a leader-based approach, and eventual consistency with reconciliation. Each is discussed in section four.
Defend a choice to use Postgres over a NoSQL database for a new service, addressing scale concerns raised by a reviewer.
Raise a non-blocking concern about API surface area in a design review, offering a concrete alternative.
As tech lead, close a design review by summarizing decisions made, open questions, and next steps.
